tagline.text: Bohol's finest waterfall, tumbling beneath terraced rice paddies

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day to a full day

children.text: A waterfall in the mountain village of Cadapdapan, in Candijay, eastern Bohol, considered the island's tallest. Green rice terraces stretch out above the falls, and combined with nearby Canawa Spring and the beaches of Anda, you can enjoy a full day of eastern Bohol's quiet nature.
Can-umantad Falls is in the mountain barangay of Cadapdapan, in the town of Candijay at the eastern tip of Bohol Island. From the capital, Tagbilaran, it's about
97km
to Candijay, on the opposite side of the island from the southwestern cluster of Bohol's main attractions. Standing about
(roughly 60 feet) tall, it's billed as Bohol's tallest waterfall, with several channels of water cascading down a broad rock face into a series of pools, large and small, stepping down like stairs.

What makes this waterfall special is the Cadapdapan Rice Terraces spread out just above it. Farmers here shaped this once-uneven hillside into paddies by hand over generations, and the curving, stacked rice paddy walls blend with the forested hills behind them, evoking the terraces of the northern Luzon Cordillera. From the viewpoint at the edge of the terraces you take in the view, then follow the steps down to reach the falls — letting you enjoy both the terraces and the falls in a single visit.

For years it was known only to villagers, but paving the road and adding viewing stairs and rest areas has turned it into a rising star of eastern Bohol. Even so, it doesn't draw crowds of group tourists the way Chocolate Hills or the Loboc River do, and on weekdays you might have the pool in front of the falls almost entirely to yourself. Facilities nearby remain simple, so the natural atmosphere is well preserved.

It's a fairly long day trip from Panglao, so most travelers stay in the eastern beach town of Anda and drop by on a half-day route. Especially recommended for travelers who prefer quiet countryside scenery over crowded tourist spots, repeat visitors to Bohol, and those touring the island by motorbike.

blocks.title: Swimming in the pool below the falls

children.text: The largest pool below the falls is turquoise, cold, and deep. You can splash around in the shallows at the edge, or put on a life vest and get close to the falls to feel the spray.
On the way down from the parking area to the falls, a series of large and small valley pools and smaller cascades line the path. It's a good idea to pick a quieter pool and rest along the way.

From the viewpoint above the falls, you can look down over the curving terraces. The scenery is especially beautiful in the green season after planting, when the rice is growing, and in the golden season when it ripens.

blocks.title: A photo walk along the paddy walls

children.text: In the soft light of early morning or late afternoon, walk along the paddy walls and you may see farmers going about their day and water buffalo at work. Since the paddies are residents' farmland, stick to the designated paths.
A cold spring in Barangay Canawa, in the same town of Candijay, famous for water so blue and clear you can see straight to the bottom. It pairs well with the falls on a day trip.

The Candijay coast has the greatest diversity of mangrove species in Bohol, said to be home to 32 of the 47 mangrove species found in the Philippines. As you pass through the coastal villages, you'll see broad stretches of mangrove forest.

The coastal and mountain roads linking Anda, Candijay, and Guindulman see little traffic and offer great scenery, making them popular with motorbike travelers. The mountain road to the falls has steep grades and sharp curves, so ride slowly.

Travel time is long, so a same-day round trip is tiring. If possible, spend a night or two in Anda and give your eastern Bohol itinerary some breathing room.

Vehicles run until late afternoon, but service gets sparse, so set out in the morning and check the return vehicle's time in advance.

20–30 minutes

The dry season from
December
through
May

, with little rain, is best for the mountain drive and swimming at the falls. During this period the water is clear and the pools turn turquoise, and the stone steps down to the falls are less slippery. In the height of the hot season,
April–May
, however, the flow can drop and the falls may thin out.
From
June
to
November

is the rainy season, when the falls carry the most water and the terraces deepen to a rich green, but after heavy rain the water turns muddy and the mountain road gets slick with mud. In some years typhoons or tropical depressions pass through in
October–December

, which can make travel along the east coast road difficult. The terraces' appearance changes with the planting and harvest cycle, so if you want to see them green, it's worth asking locally in advance when the rice will be growing. Within the day, the soft light of
is best for both photos and swimming.

There's almost no lodging near the falls, so it's best to stay in the beach town of Anda, about
30–40 minutes
away by car. Anda has everything from guesthouses along Quinale Beach (about
a night) to clifftop resorts (about
), letting you combine the falls with cave pools and beach time. Candijay and neighboring Guindulman also have a few simple inns.

Around the falls and rice terrace viewpoint are a few simple eateries and stalls selling rice, grilled meat, instant noodles, and drinks. Options are limited, so it's also worth buying a packed lunch and fruit at the Candijay or Anda market to eat at a hut. In the coastal villages of eastern Bohol, freshly caught grilled fish and squid, and kinilaw cured in vinegar, are common, and calamay, the sticky-rice sweet from southern Bohol's Jagna served in a coconut shell, makes a good snack to pack along.
Opening hours generally run from about
6 AM
to around
5–6 PM
. Arrive early in the morning and you'll find fewer people and better light.
Entrance fees, habal-habal rides, and meals are all cash only, and there's no ATM nearby, so bring plenty of small bills from Anda or Tagbilaran.
The stone steps and rocks down to the falls are wet and slippery, so wear aqua shoes or strap sandals.
Self-appointed guides sometimes offer their services at the falls, but the path is simple enough that a guide isn't really necessary. If you do use one, agree on the fee first.

Canawa Spring, the rice terraces, and the falls are all close together, so it's efficient to see them in one trip, and it's convenient to negotiate a round-trip rate covering all three with your motorbike driver.
Phone signal is weak in this mountain village, so download offline maps in advance.
If you miss the last bus back, lodging is hard to find, so on a same-day round trip, be back in Candijay town before
3 PM
After heavy rain, the valley's water can rise suddenly and turn murky, so don't enter the water if the level is high or if the caretaker stops you.
The pool right below the falls is deep and cold, so if you're not a confident swimmer, wear a life vest and stay at the edges.
Before jumping from any rock, always check the water depth and for rocks below the surface.
The mountain road to the falls is steep with many sharp curves and sees frequent motorbike accidents, so avoid riding right after rain.
The rice terraces are residents' livelihood, so be careful not to walk into the paddies or damage the paddy walls.
Entrance fees and how the site is run can change depending on the village, so check the on-site signage.
